* Declare and consume CSS Custom Properties for runtime-swappable theming, including scoping and calc() combos

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED
sections.content:
* Declaring custom properties (--variable-name) at :root and scoped to selectors; var() with fallback values; runtime vs compile-time (Sass/Less) variables; theming with custom properties; cascading/inheritance behavior; combining with calc()
* @layer syntax and layer ordering; layer precedence (later-declared wins regardless of specificity); unlayered vs layered styles; why Tailwind/shadcn use @layer internally; practical layering (reset → base → components → utilities)
* *.module.css convention and automatic scoping; composing classes (composes:); CSS Modules with dynamic class names in JS/JSX; when CSS Modules beat utility-first CSS; limitations (no true dynamic values without JS interpolation)
* Block, Element, Modifier naming (.block__element--modifier); why BEM exists (specificity/naming collisions at scale); BEM's tradeoffs (verbosity vs predictability); BEM vs utility-first CSS philosophy

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED
sections.content:

* When to reach for Zustand vs Context vs server state: client-only UI state → Zustand/local state; rarely-changing app-wide values → Context; anything from the server → Stage 2, not Zustand (the most common state-management mistake)

Weak areas: Flag honestly, from the Day 272 weekly checkpoint's logged gaps and any new ones surfaced during today's final re-verification — carry these forward explicitly rather than assuming Phase 13's completion resolved them. CSS Houdini in particular (Day 270) is the phase's most niche topic and the one most likely to need a refresher before being asked about it cold.
Improvement plan: Carry Confluence Lite forward unchanged into whichever phase comes next, the same way ClientSync/Meridian/Watchtower/Concourse/Sage have been carried forward and re-verified at every prior exit point. Continue periodic re-verification of Confluence Lite's real-time and offline components specifically, since silent breakage here — a Hocuspocus server left unpatched, a stale search index after a large document edit — is exactly the kind of failure this phase's own capstone was designed to teach vigilance against.

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED

sections.title: YESTERDAY REVIEW / ACTIVE RECALL

sections.title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
sections.content:
* Understand why 'unsafe-inline' defeats CSP and how a nonce‑based policy mitigates XSS
* Implement a strict nonce‑based CSP header in a Next.js/Express app
* Explain the JWT algorithm confusion attack and how algorithm pinning prevents it
* Implement JWT algorithm pinning in your auth code

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED
sections.content:
* CSP recap from Helmet.js (Phase 05) — default policies; limitations of 'unsafe-inline'
* Nonce generation per request (cryptographically random, single-use)
* Attaching the nonce to the CSP header and to script tags (in server‑rendered HTML)
* Testing CSP with CSP Evaluator (to be covered next day)
* JWT algorithm confusion: if the server accepts 'none' or an unexpected algorithm, an attacker can forge tokens
* Pinning: explicitly define allowed algorithms (e.g., only 'HS256' or 'RS256') and reject any token whose 'alg' header doesn't match
* Implementing in Node.js with jose (or jsonwebtoken) by checking the header's algorithm before verification

sections.title: RESOURCES (OFFICIAL DOCS)

* OWASP — "JWT Security" talk

sections.title: HANDS-ON CODING
sections.content:
* In your Next.js or Express app, generate a nonce per request and set it in both the CSP header and any inline <script> tags that need it (use a custom Document component in Next.js).
* Use a CSP evaluator to verify the policy is strict and blocks inline scripts without the correct nonce.
* In your JWT verification middleware, explicitly check the 'alg' header against an allowlist (e.g., 'HS256' only) and reject any token with a different or missing algorithm; test by intentionally passing a token with 'alg': 'none' and confirm it's rejected.

sections.title: PRACTICE PROBLEMS
sections.content:
* Write a CSP policy that allows scripts from your own domain, a CDN, and inline scripts with a nonce, but blocks all other sources.
* Attempt to inject a malicious script (using a browser console) and see it blocked by the CSP.
* Modify your JWT verification to accept only 'RS256' (if using asymmetric) and test with a token signed with 'HS256' to ensure rejection.

Topic: Cache-Aside Caching, Write-Through Caching

sections.title: YESTERDAY REVIEW / ACTIVE RECALL

sections.title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
sections.content:

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED
sections.content:
* Cache‑aside: application code checks cache first, on miss reads from DB and populates cache, on write invalidates or updates cache
* Write‑through: writes go to cache first, then to DB synchronously; ensures cache is always up‑to‑date
* Tradeoffs: cache‑aside offers better write performance (lazy), but risk of stale reads; write‑through ensures consistency but adds write latency
* Use cases: cache‑aside for read‑heavy, mostly static data; write‑through for data that is read frequently immediately after write

* Microsoft Patterns & Practices — Cache‑Aside

* Implement write‑through for a write endpoint (e.g., PUT /products/:id) that updates cache and DB.
* Measure latency for both patterns under load.

sections.title: YESTERDAY REVIEW / ACTIVE RECALL

sections.title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES

* Implement optimistic locking using a version column (or timestamp) to prevent lost updates

* Understand the tradeoffs: optimistic for low contention, pessimistic for high contention
* Know when to use each in a multi‑user application

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED
sections.content:
* Optimistic locking: read a row with a version, update only if version matches, increment version; if version mismatch, abort and retry
* Pessimistic locking: lock the row for the duration of the transaction, preventing others from modifying it
* Implementation in Prisma: using `@updatedAt` or a separate `version` field; using `$transaction` and `$queryRaw` for SELECT FOR UPDATE
* Tradeoffs: optimistic has less overhead but requires retry logic; pessimistic prevents conflicts but can cause deadlocks and reduce concurrency

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED

* Saga: a sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating transaction
* Choreography: each service publishes events that trigger the next step, no central coordinator
* Orchestration: a central coordinator (saga orchestrator) tells each service what to do
* Compensating transactions: undo the effects of a previous step if a later step fails
* Use case: order processing with multiple services (payment, inventory, shipping)

* States: Closed (normal), Open (failing fast), Half‑Open (testing if service recovered)
* Implementation patterns: using a library (e.g., opossum) or custom with Redis
* Integration with observability: monitoring circuit breaker state and DLQ size

sections.title: YESTERDAY REVIEW / ACTIVE RECALL

* Flashcard: one-sentence definition of tenant isolation.

sections.title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
sections.content:
* Understand the three common approaches to multi‑tenancy: separate databases, separate schemas, shared schema with tenant ID
* Implement row‑level multi‑tenancy in a database (using a tenant_id column)
* Enforce tenant isolation at the application and database levels
* Design a tenant‑aware caching strategy

sections.title: CONCEPTS COVERED
sections.content:
* Multi‑tenancy: a single instance of the application serves multiple tenants (customers)
* Approaches: separate DB (highest isolation, most expensive), separate schemas, shared schema (lowest isolation, cheapest)
* Row‑level isolation: every table has a tenant_id; all queries must filter by it
* Application‑level: ensure the tenant is set in the context (e.g., from JWT) and used in every query
* Database‑level: use Row Level Security (RLS) in PostgreSQL to enforce isolation automatically
* Tenant‑aware caching: cache keys should include tenant_id to avoid data leakage
